Galloping Granny

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Meet Deirdre Larkin, the 85 year old who runs faster than you do

Unique Selling Point:
Dieirdre Larkin started running at the age of 78. Born with a missing vertebra she never exercised throughout her life. When a doctor told her to exercise for her osteoarthritis, she took up running. Within a few years she had smashed the 10km World record for her age group.

Summary:
Meet Charles Eugster, a retired dentist who took up weight training at the age of 87. He is now a regular motivational speaker on TED talks, holds multiple world records in the 90 to 95 age group, and has just published his book: "Age is Just a Number" Described as an expert in successful ageing, Charles has been interviewed on BBC Breakfast, Channel 5, Radio 4, BBC World Service, and featured in The Telegraph, The Sunday Times, the Daily Express and Yahoo Sport UK - all this week.

Further information:
We speak to gerontologist Dr Brent Tipping about the latest research in ageing, and how exercise impacts positively on geriatric health - no mater what age you start. This will be an inspirational story, but also one that will encourage ordinary viewers to get up and start exercising, because the benefits will be so obvious.

Press Release:


Age is Just a Number
The first time Deirdre Larkin laced up to go for a run back in 2009 she managed only a few steps. Despite a lifetime of inactivity and being a 78-year osteoporosis sufferer, her determination paid off. Now, at 85, she’s run countless races and has just broken a world record by a whopping 20 minutes! How does 97-year-old Charles Eugsters keep his fit and lean body looking like that of a man half his age? Carte Blanche meets old people with bodies that defy their chronological age. What is their secret to longevity?


Script:


ACTIVE AGEING

V/O: At the age of 97 Charles Eugster is known as the world’s fittest pensioner. This retired dentist from Switzerland had always been a keen rower, but 10 years ago he took his fitness up a notch.

Charles: I joined a bodybuilding club at the age of 87 I think, and employed a previous Mr Universe. He said he wanted to make me stage worthy.

V/O: Within a year, Charles had lost 12kg and was soon showing off his new muscles.

Sfx: Wakeboarding

V/O: This was also the age he tried wakeboarding for the first time.
He won 4 world titles for bodybuilding, but that was just the beginning.

Charles: At the age of 90 I was able to find a job. I was employed by one of the biggest fitness groups in Germany; at 93 I decided to become a speaker, I gave a TED X talk. And then at the age of 95 I decided to become a sprinter and at 96 was able to establish 2 world records, and at the age of 97 for the first time in my life I decided to become an author. In other words you can start something new at any age, you can learn something new at any age, you can start a new life at any age.

V/O: His first book “Age Is Just A Number” hit the shelves last month. Charles believes we have to change our attitude towards old age.

Charles: Retirement is the main incubator for chronic disease, simply because retirement is voluntary or involuntary unemployment. The most important factor of successful ageing is work, the second is nutrition and number 3 is exercise.

V/O: And Charles has his work cut out for him.

Charles: What really occupies me now is research on old age. Above the age of 70 there is very little research. We as an older group, we are neglected by research. We are discriminated against: we have no jobs, and we’ve got no girlfriends. Look the dating agencies only produce young girls up to the age of 70.

V/O: Next month Charles will be competing in the British athletics championships, as well as the World Indoor Masters Regatta in South Korea.
Not everyone can be a world champion, but just because you’re getting older doesn’t mean you have to become frail, according to medical doctor Frances Fleming.

Frances: There’s a condition called sarcopenia which means a natural loss of muscle strength and mass and that process starts in all of us, in about our mid 30s, But we used to think that it was an inevitable process, we now know from the studies that loss of muscle to the extent that we used to think that it is inevitable is not so, and that we can protect our muscle mass as we get older.

Derek: Give us an example of exercises we should do?

Frances: There’s more emphasis on strength training, on resistance training, weight training of some sort to try and keep the muscle bulk and strength good.

Link: Active ageing is the new buzzword; no matter how old you are or how old you feel, it’s never too late to get up, get active and lead a full life.

Hannah: A lot of clients battle with walking and balance. So we need to look at ways of getting them to move more effectively, and be able to functionally balance thorough dynamic balance training programs.

V/O: Biokineticist Hannah Raath has a special interest in older adults.

Hannah: The quality of your life is very important. You can be an old 65 or you can be a young 90 year-old. It’s all about your limitations and how much you challenge yourself.

V/O: Randburg’s Joan Gerber is 76 years-old. She dances 5 days a week, for an hour, and is the South African Champion for Silver Masters in Latin and Ballroom.

Joan: It makes you think. You have to remember all the steps.

Derek: And do the years take their tally?

Joan: Of course they do! I’ve had a hip replacement.

Derek: And how has that affected your dancing?

Joan: Not at all, not at all.

Derek: What about friends of yours, have you encouraged them to take up ballroom dancing?

Joan: Well lots of my friends are dead already, but the younger ones I meet I tell them all.

Link: If you’re lucky enough to reach the age of 85, just walking the dog around the block could be quite an achievement but how about working 5 days a week and breaking records over the weekend.

V/O: Randburg’s Deirdre Larkin gets up at five o’ clock every morning to exercise. Her punishing routine includes weight resistance training for her whole body. Born missing a vertebra, she’d never done any strenuous exercise, but when she was diagnosed with osteoporosis at the age of 78, she decided to get active.

Deirdre: I’ve tried yoga, it’s boring; I’m no good at tennis – my racquet’s got a permanent hole in it. And I thought I’ll try running. And I started kind of three steps, three runs, three steps, three runs. For about two weeks and gradually I got better.

V/O: So much better that within four years she had broken the South African 10k record for women over 70, in a time of 54 minutes and 17 seconds. She also smashed the world record for women over eighty.

Derek: What has running actually brought to your life?

Deirdre: Excitement every weekend – I get very excited about the races.

V/O: She runs 5 days a week and does at least one race every weekend. After only 7 years on the road her medals room is filling up.

Deirdre: Don’t know where to put them so I’m using coat hangers for the rest of the medals.

Derek: Oh so this is the overflow rack hey?

Deirdre: It’s fun, the more you get the more you enjoy it.

V/O: Last weekend Deirdre drove herself to Pretoria at half past three in the morning to compete in a half marathon. Dwarfed by other runners at the start she quickly set her own pace and was difficult to keep up with.

Derek: Deirdre do you know how fast you were running?

Deirdre: No, no. I just hoped for the best. I had no idea – not until I saw the clock.

V/O: Not only did she run her personal best, she broke the world record for women 85 years and older. She finished in 2 hours 12 minutes and 45 seconds, smashing the previous world record by over 20 minutes. But the organizers didn’t realize it – and neither did Deirdre.

Deirdre: Three years ago I did it in 2:18. So I’ve improved.

Derek: Do you know that you broke the world record?

Deirdre: Did I?

Derek: By more than twenty minutes. Would you like to compete in a half marathon overseas?

Deirdre: Ooh, I’d love to, yes, I’d love to – somewhere or other. But it’s too expensive. As it is I’m living very comfortably because I’ve got a job. If I didn’t have a job, I wouldn’t be able to do the races. I couldn’t afford all the petrol and the clothes and stuff.

V/O: Deirdre is a former concert pianist and teaches at St Peter’s College in Sandton. She gives lessons every day and gets home at 7’o clock at night.

Derek: Many people over 65 are on some sort of medication, sometimes chronic medication. What about yourself?

Deirdre: No, nothing at all, no. I never take anything except vitamins.

Derek: So how do you ward off osteoporosis?

Deirdre: Well I haven’t been back for a test to see how my bones have improved, but I tell people my bones are full of holes, that’s why I run so fast.

























ACTIVE AGEING PROMOS

Promo 1 (10”)

Derek: Age is just a number, we meet 2 world champions breaking records into their 80s and 90s.

Promo 2 (15”)

Derek: Deidre Larkin is breaking world running records at 85 and she only hit the road 7 years ago, she reveals her fitness recipe.

Deirdre: The older you get, the more you need to use whatever limbs you’re left with.

Promo 3: (15”)

V/O: Meet Charles Eugster

Derek: Having achieved so much by the age of 97, you would think that Charles would finally be hanging up his sprinting shoes but he’s writing books and making big plans for the future.
